**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard my name spoken in a language I didn’t understand, I was twelve. It was in a small café in Marrakech, where the air smelled of spiced tea and old books. A woman with silver-streaked hair—her fingers stained with henna—had called me by it in Arabic, soft and deliberate, as if testing the sound of it on her tongue. I didn’t know then that names carry weight, that they can be both a key and a lock, that they can open doors or slam them shut.

My name, *Layla*, means "night" in Arabic, but it also means "delicate" in Persian. I was never delicate. Not in the way the world expected. I was the girl who climbed trees until her knees bled, who stayed up until dawn reading books about stars and black holes, who argued with my father about the injustice of gravity. He would sigh and say, *"You are too much, my little storm."* And I would smile, because I knew he meant it as a compliment.

But names aren’t just sounds. They’re histories. My mother’s name, *Fatima*, was the name of the Prophet’s daughter, a woman of quiet strength. My grandfather’s name, *Abdullah*, meant "servant of God," though he served no god but himself—he was a tailor who stitched dreams into fabric, who taught me that even the smallest stitch could hold the weight of a memory. My uncle’s name, *Khalid*, meant "eternal," though he died before he turned thirty, leaving behind a wife who still wears his ring on her left hand, the one she never took off.

Names are also promises. My best friend, *Nadia*, swore she would always be there when I needed her. She kept that promise until the day she moved to Canada, until the day her voice stopped reaching me across the ocean. Now, when I hear her name, it’s like a half-remembered song—familiar, but just out of reach.

I once met a man in Istanbul who told me his name was *Yusuf*, which meant "God will increase." He was a poet, and he said that names were like seeds—some grew into towering trees, others withered before they could take root. I asked him if he thought my name would grow. He smiled and said, *"Names don’t grow, Layla. They are. They are the shape of the hand that writes them."*

I think about that sometimes. About the hands that have written my name—my mother’s looping script on my birth certificate, my father’s rough, impatient scrawl on the back of a postcard, the stranger’s in the café who didn’t know me but still spoke it like a prayer.

Names are also the things people forget. My grandmother’s name was *Aisha*, but no one called her that anymore. They called her *Ammi*, "mother," as if the name itself had faded like an old photograph. I wonder if that’s what will happen to me. If one day, someone will say my name and then forget it, as if it were never spoken at all.

But names can also be weapons. The day I turned eighteen, my father gave me a new name—*Leila*, the softer version, the one that sounded like a sigh. He said it was because I was "ready to be gentle." I didn’t tell him that I had already been gentle for years, that I had spent my whole life being the one to hold things together, the one to listen, the one to swallow my own needs so others wouldn’t have to feel the weight of theirs.

I kept both names. *Layla* for the nights I climbed into my bed and cried, for the days I stood under the stars and felt like I was made of stardust. *Leila* for the times I had to be small, for the moments I had to pretend I wasn’t the storm.

Names are the first things we lose and the last things we keep. They are the echoes of who we were before we knew we had to be something else.

I wonder what my name will sound like when I’m old. Will it be whispered like a secret, or shouted like a command? Will it be the name of a woman who was loved, or the name of a woman who was forgotten?

For now, I am *Layla*. I am the night. I am the girl who still believes in the impossible, who still thinks the world is made of stories waiting to be told.

And if someone asks me my name, I will tell them. Not because it’s who I am, but because it’s the closest thing I have to a map. A map of the places I’ve been, the places I’m going, and the places I’ll never see again.

---
